topic.name: Reducing a Quadratic Curve to Its Principal Axes

question.text: Find the principal axes of the curve $2x_1^2-4x_1x_2+5x_2^2 = 1.$
question.explanation:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2-4x_1x_2+5x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1 \]

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=6 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=1.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=6,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 6 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} - 6 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 1 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} - 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve

question.text: Find the principal axes of the curve $9x_1^2+8x_1x_2-6x_2^2 = 5.$
question.explanation:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=9x_1^2+8x_1x_2-6x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 5 \]

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=10 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=-7.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 10 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6 \end{bmatrix} - 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ 4 & -16 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{17},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-7,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-7) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6 \end{bmatrix} + 7 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{17},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve

question.text: Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$ and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=10$ and $\lambda_2=5,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 3 \]

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 10 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues

question.text: Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=2$ and $\lambda_2=-3,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 7 \]

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=2,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 2 I &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} -2 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-3,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-3) I &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues

question.text: Which curve is defined by the equation $3x_1^2-6x_1x_2-5x_2^2 = 24?$
question.explanation:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=3x_1^2-6x_1x_2-5x_2^2.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ -3 & -5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I | &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 3 - \lambda & -3 \\ -3 & -5 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2 + 2 \lambda - 24 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 4, \, -6 \end{align*}

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $4y_1^2 - 6y_2^2.$

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

\[ \begin{align*} 4y_1^2 - 6y_2^2 &= 24 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{6} - \dfrac{y_2^2}{4} &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{(\sqrt6)^2} - \dfrac{y_2^2}{2^2} &= 1 \end{align*} \]

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt6$ and $2.$
